Chapter 8: Embedding Coaching in Team Culture—From Individual Habit to Collective Practice.
You know, while it’s powerful when one leader starts using a coaching approach, something truly remarkable happens when coaching becomes part of the team’s DNA. That’s when you see real change—not just a handful of good conversations, but a shift that runs through day-to-day work, decision-making, and even your team’s values.
Imagine a coaching culture where curiosity and reflection aren’t just buzzwords, but a natural part of every meeting and interaction. It’s a place where team members feel safe to ask questions, open up about challenges, and try out new ideas—even if they might not work out perfectly. And leaders? They set the tone by being open about what they don’t know and inviting everyone else to weigh in.
So, how can you help make this kind of culture a reality? Here are some practical steps worth trying:
First, make coaching conversations feel normal. Don’t just leave it to managers—encourage everyone to use those essential coaching questions in meetings, during check-ins, or when you’re solving problems together.
Next, celebrate learning and experimentation. Shout out the folks who try new things, even if the results are a little uncertain. It sends the message that growth and trying are just as important as hitting the mark every time.
When giving feedback, approach it with curiosity. Think of it as a joint exploration—maybe ask, “What was most useful for you?” rather than just giving a top-down critique. It makes feedback a two-way street.
And don’t forget to build coaching into your routines. Maybe carve out time during team meetings for reflection, peer coaching, or just sharing insights. Small changes like these can really add up.
Here’s what this looks like in action: picture a team that starts each weekly meeting by asking, “What’s on your mind?” That Kickstart Question becomes an open door for honest conversations and shared problem-solving. Over time, the team starts trusting each other more, and everyone’s voice gets heard.
When coaching becomes a collective habit, the whole team gets stronger. You’ll notice more adaptability, creativity, and resilience. People tackle challenges together and celebrate wins as a group. The leader’s role shifts—from being the one with all the answers to guiding the team’s learning and growth.
Of course, building this kind of culture takes time. It’s not something that changes overnight. It needs steady modeling, encouragement, and support from everyone—not just the top. But if you stick with it, the payoff is huge: a team that’s more engaged, empowered, and ready to perform at its best.
